passages.t: A yoke for the nations' envoys
passages.happening:
At the beginning of Zedekiah's reign, God tells Jeremiah to make a yoke of straps and bars and put it on his neck (verse 2). He is to send word to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon through their envoys who have come to Zedekiah in Jerusalem (verse 3).

The message is this. ‘By My great power and outstretched arm, I made the earth and the men and beasts on the face of it, and I give it to whom I please’ (verse 5). God has given all these lands to his servant Nebuchadnezzar (verse 6). ‘All nations will serve him and his son and grandson, until the time of his own land comes’ (verse 7).

The nation that will not bow its neck under Babylon's yoke, God will punish with sword, famine and plague (verse 8). They must not listen to their prophets, diviners, dreamers, mediums and sorcerers who say they will not serve Babylon (verse 9). Those lies will remove them from their land (verse 10). But the nation that bows under the yoke will stay in its own land and farm it (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The BSB dates this word to Zedekiah's reign. Most Hebrew manuscripts read Jehoiakim in verse 1, while the Greek lacks the verse; the BSB follows a few manuscripts and the context, since verses 3 and 12 name Zedekiah and 28:1 places the next events in the same year.

The envoys of the small kingdoms around Judah had apparently gathered to plan a revolt against Babylon. Jeremiah walked into their meeting wearing an ox yoke.

A yoke was a wooden bar laid across the necks of two oxen and tied on with straps, so they could pull a plow or cart. It was a common picture of being subject to a master or an empire. Jeremiah's yoke was a sign acted out in public. His message to the foreign kings was that the God of Israel made the earth and gives it to whom he pleases, even to Babylon, for a time.
passages.later: Daniel says of God, ‘He removes kings and establishes them’ (Daniel 2:21). The next chapter tells how the prophet Hananiah broke this yoke from Jeremiah's neck (Jeremiah 28:10).
passages.asks: Jeremiah wore a yoke into a meeting of kings plotting revolt. Ask whether you believe God rules over the powers of your own day. And ask what it would mean to trust God's timing when every voice around you says to act now.

passages.t: Serve the king of Babylon and live
passages.happening:
Jeremiah gives Zedekiah the same message: put your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serve him and his people, and live (verse 12). Why should the king and his people die by sword, famine and plague (verse 13)? They must not listen to the prophets who say they will not serve Babylon, for those prophets speak lies (verse 14). God did not send them (verse 15).

To the priests and people Jeremiah says not to listen to the prophets who promise that the temple's vessels will soon come back from Babylon (verse 16). “Serve the king of Babylon and live! Why should this city become a ruin?” (verse 17). If those prophets are true, let them pray that the vessels still left in the temple and the palace do not go to Babylon too (verse 18).

For the pillars, the bronze sea, the stands and the rest of the vessels left behind when Jeconiah was taken (verses 19 and 20) will be carried to Babylon and stay there ‘until the day I attend to them again,’ declares the LORD, ‘Then I will bring them back and restore them to this place’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The temple vessels had been taken in 597 BC with Jehoiachin. The false prophets said they would return soon. Jeremiah says the rest will follow them to Babylon, and only later, in God's time, will they come home.

The bronze pillars and the great bronze basin called the sea were the huge works of Solomon that stood in the temple court. Kings records that they were broken up and carried to Babylon in 586 BC.

Jeremiah's counsel to surrender was not a general rule about politics. It rested on a particular word from God about a particular empire for a limited time, given to a nation under judgment. Babylon itself was not righteous, and the book announces its fall.
passages.later: Ezra records the return of the vessels under Cyrus: ‘King Cyrus also brought out the articles belonging to the house of the LORD’ (Ezra 1:7). Kings tells how the bronze pillars were broken up and carried off (2 Kings 25:13).
passages.hard:
Was Jeremiah telling his people to collaborate with a tyrant? Does God always want submission to an oppressor?

In his own day many saw Jeremiah as a defeatist or a traitor (37:13-14). But his counsel rested on a particular word from God about a particular empire for a limited time (verse 7; 25:11-12), given to a nation under judgment. Babylon was not righteous; Jeremiah also announced its punishment (chapters 50 and 51). Some readers draw the principle that God's people should not put their hope in revolt or national survival. Others warn against turning a particular command into a rule for every situation, noting that Scripture also honors resistance to tyranny elsewhere, such as the midwives in Exodus 1 and Daniel's friends in Daniel 3.

The chapter clearly teaches that God, not the empire and not national pride, decides the times. It is not a rule that anyone must submit to oppression, and these notes draw no line from it to any nation or government of the present day.
passages.asks: Jeremiah's word was for one moment and one empire. Ask how you tell the difference between a word for a particular time and a rule for all times. And ask where your hope rests when powers rise and fall.
